title: HOME
blurb: A roof, a door, dinner and something to wear.

radicals.name: ROOF
radicals.cnLit: the lid on the character 宝
radicals.origin: The outline of a house: a ridge on top and two walls coming down. It is never used alone and always sits on top.
radicals.clue: houses and what is kept indoors
ex: a pig 豕 under the roof: a household with food
radicals.watch: Two look-alikes. 冖 (a cover) has no dot on top: 写 (to write). 穴 (a cave) has two extra legs: 空 (empty), 窗 (window).

radicals.name: DOOR
radicals.origin: The traditional form 門 is a pair of swinging saloon doors. The simplified 门 keeps the frame, and the rest of the character stands in the doorway.
ex: sunlight 日 through a gap in the door
a horse 马 charging through the gate
a person 人 glimpsed in a doorway
radicals.watch: In 问 (wèn, to ask) and 闻 (wén, to hear) the door is the sound part: mén, wèn, wén. The meaning is carried by what stands inside, a mouth 口 and an ear 耳.

radicals.name: FOOD
radicals.origin: 食 is a lid over a full bowl of grain. Simplified Chinese writes it in three strokes when it stands on the left.
radicals.watch: 馆 (guǎn) first meant an inn that fed travellers. Now it names many public buildings: 饭馆 (restaurant), and also 图书馆 (library).

radicals.name: CLOTHES
radicals.origin: 衣 is a robe with a collar and two wide sleeves. On the left it folds up into five strokes.
radicals.watch: The classic mix-up: 衤 (clothes) has two short strokes on its right side. 礻 (spirit, altar) has only one, as in 礼 (ceremony) and 神 (god).

radicals.name: SILK
radicals.origin: A twisted skein of silk thread with its loose ends hanging down. Simplified Chinese writes the ends as one rising stroke.
radicals.watch: Colours came from dyed silk, so 红 (red), 绿 (green) and 紫 (purple) all carry it. In 给 (gěi, to give) and 经 (jīng, to pass through) the thread is hard to see now.
